questions.scenario: After a teacher files a sexual harassment complaint against a principal, the principal tells the school board: 'I'm the one being harassed — she's ruining my reputation and my career is the real victim here.' This pattern has a name. What is it?
options: Legitimate counter-complaint
DARVO
Whistleblower protection claim
questions.reveal: DARVO stands for Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. The accused denies the behavior, attacks the credibility of the person reporting, then positions themselves as the real victim. It's one of the most commonly used tactics to derail accountability processes.
questions.citation: Harsey, S.J., Zurbriggen, E.L., & Freyd, J.J. (2017). Perpetrator Responses to Victim Confrontation: DARVO and Victim Self-Blame. Journal of Aggression, Maltreatment & Trauma.

questions.scenario: DARVO is effective even when the reversal is implausible. Why?
options: Because investigators are legally required to treat all parties equally, regardless of evidence
Because it shifts the emotional and administrative burden onto the reporter — who now must also defend themselves
Because most institutions have no policy for handling counter-complaints
questions.reveal: When an abuser reverses victim and offender, the original reporter suddenly has to manage two processes: their own complaint and the counter-allegation against them. The emotional labor, credibility scrutiny, and procedural costs double — which often causes reporters to withdraw.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J. (2020). Institutional courage as an antidote to institutional betrayal. In B. Hamber & E. Palmary (Eds.), Trauma, Peacebuilding and Development.

questions.scenario: A colleague tells you their abuser is now claiming to be the victim. Your colleague is scared and thinking of dropping their complaint. What would be most helpful?
options: Encourage them to drop it to avoid further conflict
Stay neutral — you can't know what really happened
Name the pattern, help document the original complaint timeline, and connect them to an advocate
questions.reveal: Recognizing DARVO doesn't mean prejudging the outcome — it means naming a known tactic so the reporter can make informed decisions. Documenting a clear timeline of the original complaint vs. the counter-allegation is protective. Advocates familiar with this pattern can help navigate the process.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J., & Birrell, P.J. (2013). Blind to Betrayal. Wiley.

share.hook: Most people have never heard of DARVO — but they've seen it happen.
share.sub: I just learned how to recognize one of the most common tactics used to silence reporters. Takes 2 minutes.

questions.scenario: A university investigates a sexual assault complaint internally rather than involving law enforcement. The survivor is later penalized academically. This is an example of:
options: Due process in action
Institutional betrayal
Standard campus policy
questions.reveal: Institutional betrayal occurs when a trusted institution causes harm — or fails to prevent it — especially after someone depends on them for protection.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J. (1994). Betrayal trauma: Traumatic amnesia as an adaptive response to childhood abuse.

questions.scenario: Why does institutional betrayal tend to cause more lasting harm than harm from a stranger?
options: Because institutions have more resources to cover up wrongdoing
Because the victim depended on the institution — betrayal by a trusted system amplifies trauma beyond the original harm
Because institutional cases take longer to resolve legally
questions.reveal: Betrayal trauma theory explains that harm inflicted by those we depend on is processed differently by the brain. The need to maintain the relationship creates a split between awareness and memory, intensifying long-term trauma symptoms compared to harm by a stranger.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J. (1996). Betrayal Trauma: The Logic of Forgetting Childhood Abuse. Harvard University Press.

questions.scenario: An employee reports harassment to HR. HR clears the respondent, and the employee is moved to a lower-visibility role. What does institutional courage look like here?
options: HR conducting the same investigation it would for any complaint
The institution proactively reviewing outcomes for signs of retaliation and publishing its findings
Leadership expressing public sympathy for the employee
questions.reveal: Institutional courage means taking bold, proactive steps — not just technically complying. It includes auditing whether reporters experience retaliation after complaints, publishing outcome data, and holding the institution publicly accountable for its own processes.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J. (2020). Institutional courage as an antidote to institutional betrayal.

share.hook: Most people can't name institutional betrayal when they experience it.
share.sub: I just learned what it is — and how to recognize it. Takes 2 minutes.

questions.scenario: A federal employee discloses evidence of contractor fraud to the agency Inspector General. Within two months, her performance reviews decline, she's excluded from key meetings, and her security clearance is flagged. This sequence is best described as:
options: Performance management
Retaliation for protected disclosure
Coincidental role changes
questions.reveal: Federal whistleblower statutes — including the Whistleblower Protection Act — define retaliation as any personnel action taken as a result of a protected disclosure. Exclusion, adverse reviews, and security clearance challenges are all recognized retaliatory patterns.
questions.citation: Merit Systems Protection Board. (2022). Whistleblower Protections for Federal Employees.

questions.scenario: Why do many whistleblowers face retaliation even when their disclosures are accurate and made through official channels?
options: Official channels don't protect disclosures about their own agency
Reporting accurate misconduct disrupts existing power structures — those structures often respond defensively regardless of legal protections
Most whistleblower laws only protect false allegations that can't be verified
questions.reveal: Legal protections exist but are difficult to enforce. Retaliation often takes subtle forms — reassignment, exclusion, changed duties — that are hard to prove in isolation. The power imbalance means whistleblowers bear most of the personal, professional, and financial cost of disclosure.
questions.citation: Government Accountability Project. (2021). Whistleblower Survival Guide.

questions.scenario: A colleague is considering reporting financial misconduct and asks what to do before disclosing. What's the most protective first step?
options: Submit the report immediately before anything can be altered
Tell their manager first to give the organization a chance to self-correct
Document the misconduct with dates and specifics, then consult a whistleblower attorney before filing
questions.reveal: Documentation protects the whistleblower as much as the disclosure itself. A whistleblower attorney can advise on which channel offers the strongest legal protection — some channels don't trigger statutory protections. Telling a manager first often accelerates retaliation and can undermine later claims.
questions.citation: National Whistleblower Center. (2023). Know Your Rights.

share.hook: Most whistleblowers don't know which channel protects them before they file.
share.sub: I just learned what the evidence says about retaliation — and how to prepare. Takes 2 minutes.

questions.scenario: Over six months, a manager consistently interrupts an employee in meetings, assigns tasks below their role, and tells others the employee is 'not a good fit.' No single incident would qualify as formal misconduct. This pattern is called:
options: Personality conflict
Workplace mobbing / targeted abuse
Performance coaching
questions.reveal: Targeted workplace abuse — sometimes called mobbing — is defined by its pattern and cumulative effect, not individual incidents. Each act alone seems minor; the sustained pattern causes significant psychological harm and is often designed to be deniable.
questions.citation: Lutgen-Sandvik, P., Tracy, S.J., & Alberts, J.K. (2007). Burned by bullying in the American workplace. Journal of Management Studies.

questions.scenario: Why do targets of workplace abuse often fail to report it?
options: Because they usually can't identify what's happening as abuse
Because workplace abuse only occurs in low-income industries
Because HR is legally required to protect them, which removes motivation to document
questions.reveal: Targets often can't name what's happening. Workplace abuse is rarely dramatic — it's exclusion, tone, ambient undermining. When someone can't name the pattern, they internalize it as a personal failure. Naming the tactic is often the first step toward reporting.
questions.citation: Namie, G., & Namie, R. (2009). The Bully at Work. Sourcebooks.

questions.scenario: You witness a colleague being systematically undermined by their supervisor. The colleague hasn't reported it. What's the most effective bystander action?
options: Report it on their behalf immediately
Ask privately if they're aware of the pattern and whether they want support documenting it
Confront the supervisor directly during a team meeting
questions.reveal: Bystander effectiveness research consistently shows that checking in privately, naming what you've observed, and asking what support is wanted is more helpful than acting on someone's behalf. Reporting without consent can remove the target's agency and sometimes escalate retaliation.
questions.citation: D'Cruz, P., & Noronha, E. (2011). The limits to workplace friendship. Employee Relations.

share.hook: Most workplace abuse is designed to be deniable — that's what makes it so hard to report.
share.sub: I just learned how to recognize the pattern. Takes 2 minutes.

questions.scenario: After a nonprofit employee raises concerns about financial irregularities, she is assigned to a satellite office, removed from email lists, and told her 'team fit' is under review. When she flags this to a board member, she's told: 'This is a performance issue, not retaliation.' Which element is the strongest indicator of retaliation?
options: Being moved to a satellite office — this is always retaliatory
The timing: all actions followed the protected disclosure and were characterized as performance issues
Being told it's a performance issue — this confirms the organization is hiding something
questions.reveal: Timing is the strongest indicator of retaliation. When a cluster of adverse actions follows a protected disclosure — especially when labeled as something else — that pattern is what investigators look for. Retaliation is rarely labeled as such; it's disguised as performance management, restructuring, or 'fit.'
questions.citation: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. (2021). Retaliation — Making it Personal.

questions.scenario: Why is 'soft retaliation' — exclusion, changed duties, isolation — particularly effective at silencing reporters?
options: Because soft retaliation is legally protected under at-will employment doctrine
Because each act is deniable and the cumulative harm is hard to prove, while the target bears daily psychological cost
Because most employees don't notice soft retaliation until it escalates
questions.reveal: Soft retaliation works because it operates below the threshold of provability while inflicting real harm. The target is left in a degraded work environment, increasingly isolated, while the organization maintains plausible deniability. The cost of fighting it often exceeds the perceived benefit.
questions.citation: Cortina, L.M., & Magley, V.J. (2003). Raising voice, risking retaliation. Journal of Occupational Health Psychology.

questions.scenario: A colleague believes they are experiencing retaliation but isn't sure. What's the most important thing to do right now?
options: File a formal complaint immediately to establish a paper trail
Say nothing and wait to see if it escalates before involving anyone
Document each incident with date, description, witnesses, and its proximity to the original disclosure — before escalating
questions.reveal: Contemporaneous documentation — written at the time of each incident — is the most protective action a target can take. Courts and investigators weight it heavily. The connection between disclosure and adverse action is the central legal test; a documented timeline makes that connection visible.
questions.citation: National Employment Law Project. (2022). Retaliation: What It Is and How to Document It.

share.hook: Most retaliation doesn't look like retaliation. That's the point.
share.sub: I just learned how to recognize and document it. Takes 2 minutes.

questions.scenario: After leaving an abusive work environment, a person finds they second-guess every professional interaction, have difficulty trusting colleagues' motives, and feel responsible for not leaving sooner. These responses are best understood as:
options: Signs of an anxiety disorder requiring clinical diagnosis
Adaptive responses to institutional trauma — normal reactions to abnormal treatment
Character weaknesses unrelated to the environment
questions.reveal: Hypervigilance, trust disruption, and self-blame are recognized trauma responses — not character flaws. They are adaptive: they developed to protect someone in a threatening environment. Naming them as normal responses to abnormal situations is a critical first step in reducing their hold.
questions.citation: Herman, J.L. (1992). Trauma and Recovery. Basic Books.

questions.scenario: Why do survivors of institutional abuse so often blame themselves for what happened?
options: Because self-blame is a cognitive shortcut that reduces the need to process complex institutional failures
Because self-blame preserves a sense of control — 'if I caused it, I can prevent it next time' — and protects attachment to the institution
Because most institutional abuse involves behaviors the survivor actually caused
questions.reveal: Betrayal trauma theory explains self-blame as a psychological strategy to preserve relationship with an institution on which someone depends. Acknowledging the institution caused harm requires confronting the loss of that safety. Self-blame, paradoxically, maintains the survivor's sense of agency.
questions.citation: Freyd, J.J., & Birrell, P.J. (2013). Blind to Betrayal. Wiley.

questions.scenario: A friend who experienced institutional betrayal says: 'I keep replaying what I should have done differently.' What response best supports recovery?
options: 'You need to stop thinking about it and move forward'
'Have you considered that you're describing a very normal response to what institutions do to people who report? You didn't cause it — the system responded the way it usually does.'
'At least you know now what to avoid in the future'
questions.reveal: Situating someone's experience within a systemic framework — 'this is what institutions typically do' — reduces isolation and self-blame more effectively than minimizing or silver-lining. Validation of the response as normal and situational is consistently supported by trauma research as a first step toward recovery.
questions.citation: van der Kolk, B. (2014). The Body Keeps the Score. Viking.

share.hook: Self-blame after institutional betrayal isn't a weakness — it's a known trauma response.
share.sub: I just learned why it happens and what actually helps. Takes 2 minutes.
